WASHINGTON (CNN) -- A distraught, sobbing Afghan Taliban member begged the court for mercy, but got none as an unmoved federal judge here Monday handed down maximum life sentences for convictions on drug trafficking and narco-terrorism charges. A guard watches over a pile of burning drugs in Kabul, Afghanistan, on June 25, 2008. Khan Mohammed, 38, of Nangarhar Province became the first person convicted and sentenced in the United States under a 2006 law that increased the penalty for a defendant found to be involved  with terrorism and distributing illegal drugs. Mohammed, who had been extradited from Afghanistan, was convicted by a jury in May of plotting a rocket attack on U.S. military forces and Afghan civilians at Jalalabad Airfield. He also was found guilty of distributing between $1 million and $3 million worth of heroin into the United States "to kill Americans as part of a jihad." Mohammed's court-appointed lawyer, conceding that "what he did was wrong," urged U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly to be lenient and sentence his client to only 20 years in prison. Then the full-bearded Mohammed, dressed in an orange jailhouse jumpsuit, addressed the judge. With tears streaming down his face, and choking back his words, he begged for only one or two years. "I have little children and a woman. They depend on me," Mohammed began. "I'm so worried about them." His lengthy emotional appeal went on to include his reason for selling opium. "In my village that's how you have to make a living. There is no house there without opium," he said. Justice Department prosecutor Matthew Stiglitz, however, urged the court to "send a message of deterrence," and warned against "the confluence of drug trafficking and terrorism." "No, he's not the Osama bin Laden of terrorism. No, he's not the Pablo Escobar of the drug world," Stiglitz told the judge. "But this is where the rubber meets the road." Bin Laden is the head of al Qaeda, while Escobar, who died in 1993, was the most powerful of Colombian drug lords. "Afghanistan is ground zero for opium, and an almost limitless source of funds to the Taliban," he argued. Kollar-Kotelly agreed fully with the prosecutors, and strongly admonished the Taliban defendant. "You were convicted 99 percent by your own words," the judge declared, as she recalled how a "courageous" Afghan police chief wore an undercover wire to record Mohammed's plotting. "The fact that no one died is only because you didn't get the missiles you wanted," she said. "In 2006, you celebrated the Americans' use of the opium. It was a jihad. You knew the damage it could cause," the judge continued. "Because of your undiluted hatred for the United States, you might well have launched other attacks had you not been arrested." She added, "Terrorists stand unique among criminals. Deterrence is very important here." Then, concluding dramatically, the judge turned directly to the defendant. "I heard your concerns for your family but no acceptance of responsibility for your action," the judge said. "Defendants often express worry for their families, but if they considered the consequences of their actions beforehand, maybe they would have acted differently."

At 38 years old, Khan Mohammed, a native of Nangarhar Province, holds the distinction of being the first individual to be found guilty and sentenced in the United States under legislation passed in 2006 that raised punishments for anyone linked to both terrorism and the trade of illegal narcotics.

Having been sent from Afghanistan to face trial, Mohammed received a guilty verdict from a jury this past May for orchestrating a planned rocket assault targeting American troops and Afghan civilians at Jalalabad Airfield. Jurors additionally determined that he had funneled heroin valued between $1 million and $3 million into the U.S., doing so "to kill Americans as part of a jihad."

Mohammed's assigned defense attorney acknowledged that "what he did was wrong," yet appealed to U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly for compassion, requesting a sentence limited to 20 years behind bars. Following this, Mohammed—sporting a full beard and clad in an orange prison uniform—spoke directly to the judge. Overcome by emotion, tears rolling down his cheeks and struggling to get his words out, he asked for no more than a year or two.

"I have little children and a woman. They depend on me," he said, opening his plea. "I'm so worried about them."

He continued with a drawn-out, heartfelt statement that touched on why he had sold opium. "In my village that's how you have to make a living. There is no house there without opium," he explained.

But Justice Department attorney Matthew Stiglitz called on the court to "send a message of deterrence," cautioning about "the confluence of drug trafficking and terrorism."

"No, he's not the Osama bin Laden of terrorism. No, he's not the Pablo Escobar of the drug world," Stiglitz said to the judge. "But this is where the rubber meets the road." Bin Laden leads al Qaeda, whereas Escobar—who died in 1993—reigned as the most dominant among Colombia's drug kingpins.

"Afghanistan is ground zero for opium, and an almost limitless source of funds to the Taliban," Stiglitz contended.

Kollar-Kotelly sided completely with the prosecution and delivered a sharp rebuke to the Taliban defendant.

"You were convicted 99 percent by your own words," the judge stated, referencing the way a "courageous" Afghan police chief had secretly worn a recording device to capture Mohammed's scheming.

"The fact that no one died is only because you didn't get the missiles you wanted," she noted.

"In 2006, you celebrated the Americans' use of the opium. It was a jihad. You knew the damage it could cause," she went on. "Because of your undiluted hatred for the United States, you might well have launched other attacks had you not been arrested."

She continued, "Terrorists stand unique among criminals. Deterrence is very important here."

Finally, in a striking close, the judge addressed the defendant face to face. "I heard your concerns for your family but no acceptance of responsibility for your action," she said. "Defendants often express worry for their families, but if they considered the consequences of their actions beforehand, maybe they would have acted differently."

Administration officials in Washington have acknowledged the challenges but emphasized that steps are being taken to streamline the system and strengthen vetting procedures.

Veterans' organizations have been among the most vocal supporters of the Afghan allies, framing the issue as a matter of national honor and credibility. **WASHINGTON (CNN)** — An Afghan man linked to the Taliban was sentenced to life in prison Thursday, becoming the first person convicted and sentenced under a 2006 U.S. law that established enhanced penalties for those who combine drug trafficking with terrorism.

Khan Mohammed, described by prosecutors as a member of the Taliban, received two concurrent life sentences after a federal jury in Washington found him guilty on charges of narco-terrorism and distribution of heroin and opium.

The conviction represents a milestone in the U.S. government's effort to prosecute the intersection of the narcotics trade and terrorist financing, particularly in Afghanistan, where officials say opium poppy cultivation has helped fund insurgent operations.

## The Case

According to prosecutors, Mohammed sold heroin and opium in the Nangarhar province of Afghanistan, knowing that the proceeds would be used to support insurgent activities. Evidence presented at trial indicated that Mohammed intended for the drugs to reach the United States.

Prosecutors also alleged that Mohammed sought to acquire rockets to attack U.S. and coalition forces, as well as targets at an airfield in Jalalabad. Recorded statements reportedly captured Mohammed expressing his intent to kill Americans.

"Let it be a jihad," Mohammed was quoted as saying in evidence presented during the trial, referring to his efforts to obtain rockets for attacks.

## The Law

The 2006 narco-terrorism statute was enacted by Congress to give federal prosecutors a specific tool to target individuals who use drug proceeds to fund terrorism. The law carries penalties that can reach up to life imprisonment.

Officials from the Drug Enforcement Administration, which played a central role in the investigation, hailed the sentencing as a significant achievement.

"This case demonstrates our commitment to attacking the nexus between drugs and terrorism wherever it exists," a DEA official said following the verdict.

## Significance

The Justice Department characterized the outcome as an important precedent, signaling that the United States would pursue individuals who threaten American security through both drug trafficking and violence, even beyond U.S. borders.

The case underscored the challenges facing coalition forces in Afghanistan, where the opium trade has long been intertwined with insurgent financing. U.S. officials have repeatedly identified the drug economy as a key source of revenue for militant groups operating in the region.

Mohammed was brought to the United States to stand trial, and his prosecution was closely watched as a test of how the narco-terrorism law would be applied in practice.

# Sinaloa Cartel Lieutenant Sentenced to 30 Years in Landmark Narco-Terrorism Case

**NEW YORK** — A federal judge on Thursday sentenced a high-ranking cartel operative to 30 years in prison, capping a years-long prosecution that authorities described as a significant blow to trafficking networks moving fentanyl and cocaine into the United States.

Ramón Delgado-Castañeda, 44, was convicted in March on charges including narco-terrorism conspiracy, drug trafficking, and firearms offenses following a six-week trial in the Southern District of New York.

## A Plea for Mercy

Speaking through a Spanish interpreter before sentencing, Delgado-Castañeda addressed the court in a quiet, halting voice, at times pausing to compose himself.

"I ask the court for mercy, not for me, but for my children who need their father," he said. "I made terrible choices because I was afraid, because there was no other way to feed my family where I come from. I am not the monster they describe. I beg your honor to let me one day return to my family."

His attorney, Marisol Vega, argued that her client played a limited operational role and had cooperated in ways that were not fully credited by prosecutors.

## The Government's Case for Deterrence

Assistant U.S. Attorney Daniel Reyes urged the court to reject that portrayal, describing the defendant as a "trusted enforcer" whose work fueled violence on both sides of the border.

"This defendant did not act out of desperation — he acted out of ambition and greed," Reyes told the court. "The poison he helped move claimed American lives in numbers we may never fully know. A sentence here must send a message that reaches every plaza boss and every trafficker who believes distance and borders will protect them. Deterrence is not abstract in a case like this. It is measured in the lives that may be saved."

## The Judge's Rebuke

U.S. District Judge Eleanor Whitfield acknowledged the defendant's family circumstances but delivered a pointed admonishment before pronouncing the sentence.

"The court has heard your words, Mr. Delgado-Castañeda, and I do not doubt that your children love you," Judge Whitfield said. "But the men and women whose families were destroyed by what you trafficked also loved their children. You had choices at every stage, and at every stage you chose the organization over human life. Fear may explain a first step. It does not explain years of committed service to an enterprise built on death."

The judge imposed the 30-year term along with five years of supervised release and ordered forfeiture of assets tied to the trafficking operation.

## Broader Context

Prosecutors said the case was the result of a multi-year investigation involving the Drug Enforcement Administration and international partners. Officials framed the outcome as part of a broader strategy targeting cartel leadership rather than low-level couriers.

"Today's sentence reflects our commitment to holding accountable those who orchestrate the flow of deadly drugs into our communities," a DEA spokesperson said in a statement following the hearing.

Defense counsel indicated they intend to appeal.

---

**Khan Mohammed becomes first person convicted under U.S. narco-terrorism statute following extradition from Afghanistan**

WASHINGTON — An Afghan national from Nangarhar Province was sentenced to life in prison after being convicted of orchestrating a rocket attack against a coalition airfield and distributing heroin with the stated intent of killing American and coalition personnel, in a case federal prosecutors described as a milestone in the intersection of drug trafficking and terrorism.

Khan Mohammed, of Nangarhar Province, Afghanistan, was convicted following his extradition to the United States—a rare legal maneuver that brought the case before a federal court in Washington, D.C. His prosecution marked the first conviction under a narco-terrorism statute that Congress enacted to target defendants who combine drug trafficking with acts of terror.

## The Charges

According to prosecutors, Mohammed engaged in a dual campaign of violence and narcotics distribution that reflected the deep connections between insurgent activity and the drug trade in eastern Afghanistan. The government presented evidence that Mohammed plotted a rocket attack targeting Jalalabad Airfield, a facility used by American and coalition forces in the region.

Separately, prosecutors charged that Mohammed distributed heroin, and that he did so with an expressed desire that the drugs reach American service members and coalition personnel. Investigators cited statements attributed to Mohammed indicating that he viewed the narcotics as a weapon against Americans—a chilling articulation of intent that formed the basis for the narco-terrorism charge.

## A First Under Federal Law

The case drew attention because it represented the first successful prosecution under the narco-terrorism statute, a law designed to reach defendants operating abroad whose drug trafficking is tied to terrorism against the United States. The statute allows American prosecutors to pursue individuals who might otherwise fall outside traditional jurisdiction, provided their conduct targets U.S. interests or personnel.

Federal officials portrayed the conviction as a demonstration that drug traffickers who align themselves with terrorist objectives can be brought to justice in American courtrooms, regardless of where their crimes occur.

## Extradition From Afghanistan

Mohammed's extradition underscored the cooperation between American and Afghan authorities during a period of intensive counterinsurgency and counternarcotics operations. His transfer to U.S. custody enabled prosecutors to try him in a federal district court, where he faced the full weight of the American criminal justice system.

The investigation involved coordination among multiple federal agencies, including the Drug Enforcement Administration, which had increasingly focused on the nexus between opium production in Afghanistan and the financing of insurgent violence.

## Significance

Officials emphasized that the case illustrated how heroin trafficking and terrorism could be fused into a single threat—one that endangered both civilian populations and the military personnel deployed to the region. The heroin trade has long served as a source of funding for insurgent operations in Afghanistan, and prosecutors argued that Mohammed embodied that convergence.

The life sentence imposed on Mohammed reflected the gravity with which the court viewed the combination of planned violence against a military installation and the deliberate use of narcotics as a means of harming Americans.

## Conclusion

The conviction and sentencing of Khan Mohammed stood as a signal case in the effort to combat narco-terrorism, establishing a legal precedent for prosecuting those who wield both drugs and violence against the United States and its allies. For federal authorities, the outcome affirmed that the reach of American law could extend to distant conflict zones where the drug trade and terrorism intersect.
